name: Kalmar Union & Denmark–Norway
summary: The Kalmar Union (1397–1523) joined Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch. After Sweden left, Denmark and Norway stayed united until 1814, ruling Iceland, Greenland and the Faroes, with small colonies in India, Africa and the Caribbean.

knownFor.label: Kronborg Castle
knownFor.note: Castle at Helsingør where ships paid the Sound Dues; the setting of Hamlet.

knownFor.label: Tycho Brahe’s observatory
knownFor.note: Uraniborg, on the island of Hven, made the most accurate observations before telescopes.

knownFor.label: Margaret I
knownFor.note: The queen who created the Kalmar Union.

location.value: Denmark (including Schleswig-Holstein and, until 1658, today’s southern Sweden), Norway, Iceland, the Faroes and Greenland.

terrain.value: Flat Danish islands and peninsula; Norway’s mountains and fjords; Atlantic islands.

climate.value: Mild and wet in Denmark; colder in Norway; Arctic in Greenland.

resources.value: Farmland, fish (cod), timber and iron from Norway, and tolls from ships in the Øresund.

disasters.value: Storm floods on the North Sea coast; the Little Ice Age; Iceland’s Laki eruption (1783) caused a famine.

urbanisation.value: Copenhagen was the largest city; Bergen and Christiania (Oslo) in Norway.

disease.value: Plague; smallpox in Iceland (1707) killed about a quarter of the people.

migration.value: Migration to Copenhagen; Danish colonists to the Caribbean and Greenland.

economicBase.value: Farming, fishing, timber exports, and the Sound Dues paid by ships passing Helsingør (1429–1857).

tradeRoutes.value: Baltic and North Sea trade; East India and West India companies.

wealth.value: The Sound Dues made the crown rich.

moneyAndTax.value: Danish rigsdaler; customs and land taxes.

inequality.value: Nobles owned much land; Danish peasants were tied to estates (stavnsbånd, 1733–1788).

governmentType.value: An elected monarchy limited by the nobles until 1660; then absolute monarchy (King’s Law, 1665).

keyRulers.value: Margaret I. Christian II. Christian IV (1588–1648). Frederick III. Christian VII (with Struensee). Frederick VI.

succession.value: Kings were elected by the nobles until 1660, then hereditary.

institutions.value: The Rigsråd (council of nobles) until 1660; then the king’s administration in Copenhagen.

stability.value: Sweden left the union in 1523 after the Stockholm Bloodbath (1520); a civil war (the Count’s Feud) in 1534–36.

eliteConflict.value: Conflict between the crown and the nobility, ended by absolutism in 1660.

armyAndTech.value: A strong navy; the Norwegian admiral Tordenskjold.

majorWars.value: Many wars with Sweden (Northern Seven Years’ War, Torstenson War, Great Northern War); bombardment of Copenhagen by Britain (1807).

territoryChange.value: Lost Scania, Halland and Blekinge to Sweden (1658); lost Norway to Sweden in 1814.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivalry with Sweden; allied with Napoleon’s France after 1807.

inventions.value: Tycho Brahe’s observations; Ole Rømer measured the speed of light (1676).

scienceEducation.value: Universities of Copenhagen (1479) and Kiel; Norway’s first university opened in 1811.

openness.value: Part of European Protestant trade and learning; strict censorship except briefly under Struensee (1770–72).

communicationTransport.value: Ships along the coasts and to Iceland and Greenland; a royal postal service (1624).

religion.value: Catholic until the Lutheran Reformation (1536); then Lutheran.

languageWriting.value: Danish was the written language in Norway too; Icelandic, Norwegian dialects and Sámi were also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Renaissance castles (Frederiksborg, Rosenborg), Ludvig Holberg’s comedies.

socialStructure.value: King, nobles, clergy, burghers and peasants; Norwegian peasants were freer than Danish ones.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king united the two kingdoms; Norwegian identity grew in the 18th century.

dailyLife.value: Timber farmhouses in Norway, brick in Danish towns; rye bread, salted fish, porridge and beer.

neighbours.value: Sweden, the German states, Britain, the Netherlands, Russia.

colonisation.value: Colonies at Tranquebar (India, 1620), the Gold Coast, and the Danish West Indies (St Thomas, St John, St Croix) with enslaved African labour; Denmark banned the slave trade from 1803.

riseSignals.value: Queen Margaret I united the three crowns at Kalmar (1397).

peakPeriod.value: Under Christian IV in the early 17th century.

declineSignals.value: Losses to Sweden in 1658 and defeat on Napoleon’s side.

outcome.value: The Treaty of Kiel (1814) gave Norway to Sweden; Denmark kept Iceland, Greenland and the Faroes.
